{{Short description|Sum of a factorial number and a triangular number}}
In [[number theory]], a '''factoriangular number''' is an [[integer]] formed by adding a [[factorial]] and a [[triangular number]] with the same index. The name is a [[portmanteau]] of "factorial" and "triangular."

== Definition ==

For <math>n \ge 1</math>, the <math>n</math>th ''factoriangular number'', denoted <math>\operatorname{Ft}_n</math>, is defined as the sum of the <math>n</math>th [[factorial]] and the <math>n</math>th [[triangular number]]:<ref name="Rayaguru">{{cite journal |last1=Rayaguru |first1=Sai Gopal |last2=Odjoumani |first2=Japhet |last3=Panda |first3=Gopal Krishna |title=Factoriangular numbers in balancing and Lucas-balancing sequence |journal=Boletín de la Sociedad Matemática Mexicana |volume=26 |pages=865–878 |date=2020-07-26 |issue=3 |doi=10.1007/s40590-020-00303-1 }}</ref>
:<math>\operatorname{Ft}_n = n! + T_n = n! + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}</math>.
The first few factoriangular numbers are:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:right;"
! <math>n</math> !! <math>n!</math> !! <math>T_n</math> !! <math>\operatorname{Ft}_n = n! + T_n</math>
|-
| 1 || 1 || 1 || 2
|-
| 2 || 2 || 3 || 5
|-
| 3 || 6 || 6 || 12
|-
| 4 || 24 || 10 || 34
|-
| 5 || 120 || 15 || 135
|-
| 6 || 720 || 21 || 741
|-
| 7 || 5,040 || 28 || 5,068
|-
| 8 || 40,320 || 36 || 40,356
|-
| 9 || 362,880 || 45 || 362,925
|-
| 10 || 3,628,800 || 55 || 3,628,855
|}

These numbers form the [[integer sequence]] [https://oeis.org/A101292 A101292] in the [[Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] (OEIS).

==Properties ==

=== Recurrence relations ===

Factoriangular numbers satisfy several [[recurrence relations]]. For <math>n \geq 1</math>,
:<math>\operatorname{Ft}_{n+1} = (n+1)\left(\operatorname{Ft}_n - \frac{n^2-2}{2}\right)</math>

And for <math>n \geq 2</math>,
:<math>\operatorname{Ft}_n = n\left(\operatorname{Ft}_{n-1} - \frac{n^2-2n-1}{2}\right)</math>

These are linear [[Recurrence relation#Solving first-order non-homogeneous recurrence relations with variable coefficients|non-homogeneous recurrence relations]] with variable coefficients of order 1.

=== Generating functions ===

The [[exponential generating function]] <math>E(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \operatorname{Ft}_n \tfrac{x^n}{n!}</math> for factoriangular numbers is (for <math>-1 < x < 1</math>)
:<math>E(x) =  \frac{2 + (2-5x^2+2x^3+x^4)e^x}{2(1-x)^2}</math> 
If the sequence is extended to include <math>\operatorname{Ft}_0 = 1</math>, then the exponential generating function becomes
:<math>E(x) = \frac{2 + (2x-x^2-x^3)e^x}{2(1-x)}</math>.

=== Representations as sums of triangular numbers ===

Factoriangular numbers can sometimes be expressed as sums of two triangular numbers:

* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_n = 2T_n</math> if and only if <math>n = 1</math> or <math>n = 3</math>.
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_n = T_x + T_n</math> if and only if <math>8n! + 1</math> is a perfect square. For <math>n \neq x</math>, the only known solution is <math>(\operatorname{Ft}_5, T_{15}) = (135, 120)</math>, giving <math>\operatorname{Ft}_5 = T_5 + T_{15}</math>.
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_n = T_x + T_y</math> if and only if <math>8\operatorname{Ft}_n + 2</math> is a sum of two squares.

=== Representations as sums of squares ===

Some factoriangular numbers can be expressed as the sum of two squares. For <math>n \leq 20</math>, the factoriangular numbers that can be written as <math>a^2 + b^2</math> for some integers <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> include:

* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_1 = 2 = 1^2 + 1^2</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_2 = 5 = 1^2 + 2^2</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_4 = 34 = 3^2 + 5^2</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_9 = 362,925 = 195^2 + 570^2</math>

This result is related to the [[sum of two squares theorem]], which states that a positive integer can be expressed as a sum of two squares if and only if its [[prime factorization]] contains no prime factor of the form <math>4k+3</math> raised to an odd power.

=== Fibonacci factoriangular numbers ===
A ''Fibonacci factoriangular number'' is a number that is both a [[Fibonacci number]] and a factoriangular number. There are exactly three such numbers:

* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_1 = 2 = F_3</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_2 = 5 = F_5</math>
* <math>\operatorname{Ft}_4 = 34 = F_9</math>

This result was conjectured by Romer Castillo and later proved by Ruiz and Luca.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gomez Ruiz|first1=C.A.|last2=Luca|first2=F.|title=Fibonacci factoriangular numbers|journal=[[Indagationes Mathematicae]]|volume=28|issue=4|year=2017|pages=796–804|doi=10.1016/j.indag.2017.05.002|hdl=21.11116/0000-0004-086E-9|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Rayaguru"/>

=== Pell factoriangular numbers ===
A ''Pell factoriangular number'' is a number that is both a [[Pell number]] and a factoriangular number.<ref name="Pell">{{cite journal |last1=Luca |first1=Florian |last2=Odjoumani |first2=Japhet |last3=Togbé |first3=Alain |title=Pell Factoriangular Numbers |journal=Publications de l'Institut Mathématique |series=Nouvelle série |volume=105 |issue=119 |year=2019 |pages=93–100 |doi=10.2298/PIM1919093L |doi-access=free }}</ref> Luca and Gómez-Ruiz proved that there are exactly three such numbers: <math>\operatorname{Ft}_1 = 2</math>, <math>\operatorname{Ft}_2 = 5</math>, and <math>\operatorname{Ft}_3 = 12</math>.<ref name="Pell"/>

=== Catalan factoriangular numbers ===

A ''Catalan factoriangular number'' is a number that is both a [[Catalan number]] and a factoriangular number. The only such numbers are 1, 2 and 5.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Catalan numbers which are factoriangular numbers |date=2024 |publisher=Florian Luca, Japhet Odjoumani and Alan Togbé |location=Mathematics Division, Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch, South Africa|pages=1—4|year=2024|language=English|url=https://publikacio.uni-eszterhazy.hu/8235/1/AMI_60_from93to97.pdf}}</ref> They also proved in the same paper that the only [[central binomial coefficients]] which are also factoriangular numbers are 1 and 2.

== Generalizations ==

The concept of factoriangular numbers can be generalized to <math>(n,k)</math>-factoriangular numbers, defined as <math>\operatorname{Ft}_{n,k} = n! + T_k</math> where <math>n</math> and <math>k</math> are positive integers. The original factoriangular numbers correspond to the case where <math>n = k</math>. This generalization gives rise to factoriangular triangles, which are [[Pascal triangle|Pascal-like triangular arrays]] of numbers. Two such triangles can be formed:

* A triangle with entries <math>\operatorname{Ft}_{n,k}</math> where <math>k \leq n</math>, yielding the sequence: 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 25, 27, 30, 34, ...
* A triangle with entries <math>\operatorname{Ft}_{n,k}</math> where <math>k \geq n</math>, yielding the sequence: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12, 11, 12, 16, 34, ...

In both cases, the diagonal entries (where <math>n = k</math>) correspond to the original factoriangular numbers.
